props.title: One of Our Dinosaurs Is Missing

sections.content: Disney's One of Our Dinosaurs Is Missing sits at a fascinating intersection of British spy capers and family-friendly adventure comedies. Set in 1920s London, it features Peter Ustinov and Helen Hayes in a delightfully absurd plot involving stolen microfilm hidden inside a dinosaur skeleton. The film follows similar DNA to other Disney live-action comedies of the era like The North Avenue Irregulars (1979) and The Apple Dumpling Gang (1975), mixing slapstick with mild espionage elements. Its portrayal of Chinese characters is problematic by today's standards, reflecting unfortunate stereotypes common in 1970s cinema.

sections.content: The film represents a specific moment in Disney's live-action filmmaking, when the studio was heavily investing in British-American co-productions. Like Bedknobs and Broomsticks (1971) and The Island at the Top of the World (1974), it attempted to capture the success of Mary Poppins (1964) by blending British settings and actors with American production values. The Natural History Museum setting provides a unique backdrop that distinguishes it from other family capers of the era.

The espionage elements, though played for laughs, connect to a broader trend of family-friendly spy films in the 1970s, including The Cat from Outer Space (1978) and The Shaggy D.A. (1976). These films offered gentle parodies of more serious spy thrillers while maintaining Disney's commitment to wholesome entertainment. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: While not as well-remembered as other Disney live-action films of the period, One of Our Dinosaurs Is Missing established a template for museum-set adventures that would influence later works like Night at the Museum (2006) and The Mummy Returns (2001). Its blend of British character actors, exotic intrigue, and family-friendly action would be refined in subsequent decades through films like Young Sherlock Holmes (1985) and The Great Muppet Caper (1981).
